The key feasibility result is now clear: we can package a native GrizOS engine for Swift, while Void supplies the persistent Linux services. Apple’s XCFramework mechanism supports that; Quest needs a separate Android/OpenXR host, and VITURE’s current SDK support is different for iPhone versus its Android/Linux/macOS targets. # GMRI | J.A.R.V.I.S. Interface Research
<text color="secondary" size="xs" weight="medium">SOURCE ACQUIRED · NOVEMBER 2, 2026</text>

<row align="start" gap={3}>
  <AsyncImage query="Bilawal Sidhu Marvel VFX Team Accidentally Created Your AI Assistant Ian Dawson YouTube video thumbnail" aspectRatio="16:9" maxWidth="180px"/>
  <box flex="1" gap={1}>
    **<Link url="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCnjreKdfN4" title="Marvel's VFX Team Accidentally Created Your AI Assistant"/>**

    Bilawal Sidhu interviewing Ian Dawson, visual-effects producer associated with the original *Iron Man* interface work.

    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Published October 24, 2025 · 14 minutes, 3 seconds</text>
  </box>
</row>

I retrieved the complete English auto-generated transcript, the timestamped subtitles, video metadata, and all nine chapter markers.

**The most consequential finding:** Dawson describes a progression from cinematic interface design to functioning spatial enterprise tools, including collaborative three-dimensional drone-flight planning and an AI-assisted equipment-repair demonstration.

That's directly relevant to GrizOS. We're not merely recreating the appearance of J.A.R.V.I.S.; we're investigating how to turn its interaction model into real, device-specific capabilities.

And I've identified the glasses you mentioned: **VITURE Pro and VITURE Luma Pro**. Both belong to the VITURE ecosystem, but their sensing capabilities differ materially. VITURE's developer documentation confirms that the Luma Pro has a passthrough camera while the original Pro does not. <Cite refs={["turn475051search3","turn475051search10"]}/>

## The architecture you're proposing

**Void underneath. GrizOS as the operating environment. A native Swift application as the container and presentation layer.**

That is technically achievable if we separate the portable GrizOS runtime from the Linux-specific parts of Void.

<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={2}>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    <text weight="medium">GrizOS Swift Application</text>
    <caption>SwiftUI · RealityKit · voice · gestures · device permissions</caption>
  </box>
  <row justify="center" align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-up-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </row>
  <box background="rgba(40,125,91,0.09)" border={{size:1,color:"rgba(40,125,91,0.35)"}} radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Embedded GrizOS Runtime**
    <caption>Identity · memory · authority · events · agents · evidence · world state</caption>
    <text color="success" size="xs" weight="medium">Portable native library / XCFramework</text>
  </box>
  <row justify="center" align="center">
    <icon name="arrow-up-down" color="secondary" size="lg"/>
  </row>
  <box background="surface-secondary" radius="lg" padding={3} align="center" gap={1}>
    **Void Linux / GrizOS Host**
    <caption>Persistent services · model execution · orchestration · synchronization</caption>
    <text color="secondary" size="xs">Local machine / Proxmox infrastructure</text>
  </box>
</box>

Apple supports packaging native libraries as XCFrameworks and distributing them as Swift packages. <Cite refs={["turn721725search0","turn721725search1"]}/> That gives us an actual embedding mechanism rather than merely displaying a remote web application.

The distinction is important: **we can embed GrizOS's operating logic inside the iPhone application, but not simply insert a running Void Linux system and give it the privileges of iOS.** The app remains subject to Apple's sandbox and lifecycle restrictions. <Cite ref="turn293841search0"/>

We would therefore compile the same portable GrizOS core for both environments: Linux on Void and Darwin on Apple devices. Dottie stays her own persistent intelligence; GrizOS controls the environment and authority boundaries, and the Aegis agents retain their separate identities.

## One operating environment, five different interfaces

| Device | GrizOS experience |
|---|---|
| **iPhone** | Primary mobile command interface, embedded runtime, voice, evidence viewer, local state |
| **Apple Watch** | Haptic notifications, rapid commands, urgent state, concise confirmations |
| **VITURE Pro** | Head-tracked spatial displays, stabilized evidence panels, voice-controlled information |
| **VITURE Luma Pro** | Similar spatial UI with camera-assisted contextual features where the host SDK permits them |
| **Meta Quest 3** | Full spatial workspace, collaborative three-dimensional maps, hand/controller interaction |

The Quest requires a native Android/OpenXR application, but the portable GrizOS core can be compiled for that environment. <Cite ref="turn721725search7"/> The Watch can exchange state and commands with the iPhone using WatchConnectivity. <Cite ref="turn897070search0"/>

The important engineering decision is that **the devices exchange structured commands, evidence and world-state updates—not rendered screens**. That allows each device to present the same underlying reality in a form suited to its capabilities.

## I built a packaging feasibility test

  <row align="center" justify="between">
    **GrizOS Portable Core — Swift Package**
    <badge color="success">8 tests passed</badge>
  </row>
  <text color="secondary" size="sm">Verified using Swift 6.2.1 on x86-64 Linux</text>
  <text size="sm">Contains a native C core, a Swift actor wrapper, tests for offline routing, simulated role decisions, duplicate-command detection, reconnection, and bounded command storage.</text>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="center" gap={2}>
    <icon name="package" color="secondary"/>
    [Download the Swift Package feasibility test](sandbox:/mnt/data/GMRI_GrizOS_Void_Swift_Portability_2026-11-02.zip)
  </row>

  </row>

This is a **working interoperability test, not a functioning GrizOS**. It verifies that native code can be called through the proposed Swift package boundary on Linux. It does not implement real agent execution, persistence, cryptographic authorization, or a spatial interface. Apple-device compilation remains untested.

## The connection back to the video

At [3:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCnjreKdfN4&t=219s), Dawson describes how the VFX team had to accommodate Robert Downey Jr.'s natural gestures rather than enforce prescribed ones.

At [7:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCnjreKdfN4&t=428s), he describes taking the concept into operational spatial interfaces, including collaborative drone-flight planning.

Those two lessons belong at the heart of GrizOS:

**The human expresses intent naturally. The operating environment resolves context and authority. Each device renders the resulting information appropriately.**

And that means the next decisive technical milestone isn't a prettier holographic interface. It's one evidence object, one authoritative state, and one command moving reliably between an embedded iPhone runtime, the Void host, and a spatial endpoint.

With that established, the visual language Dawson describes becomes functional rather than cinematic imitation.

Oh, **this absolutely belongs in the same research corpus.** And it adds something important that Ian Dawson's interview didn't: a proposed engineering architecture underneath the J.A.R.V.I.S. interface.

I read Phil J. Łaszkowicz's entire *Stark Industries Case Study: A Technology Stack Case Study*.

There is one crucial provenance distinction: Łaszkowicz explicitly calls his 2017 article a mostly satirical exercise, based on his enterprise technology experience. It is a hypothetical reconstruction, not a disclosure of Marvel's actual software architecture. <FileCite ref="turn0file0" line_range_start={30} line_range_end={42}/>

## What the article contributes to GrizOS

| Article's proposed system | GrizOS engineering translation |
|---|---|
| **Proprietary C/C++ AI core** | Portable native runtime callable from Swift and other host applications |
| **Distributed J.A.R.V.I.S.** | Dottie, independently operating Aegis agents, and persistent host services |
| **Lightweight intelligence inside the suit** | Device-resident execution with offline operation and synchronization |
| **Centralized processing in the cloud** | Void Linux host running persistent computation and orchestration |
| **ARM processors and specialized subsystems** | Device-specific execution for iPhone, Watch, glasses, and Quest |
| **Qt, OpenGL, Vulkan spatial interfaces** | Native SwiftUI, RealityKit where supported, and OpenXR-compatible rendering |
| **Separate enterprise systems** | Institutional services, storage, permissions, and evidence management |

The article's strongest architectural proposition appears in **“The Suit.”** Łaszkowicz suggests that the suit would run a lightweight J.A.R.V.I.S. component while more extensive capabilities remain centralized, with failover and network redundancy. <FileCite ref="turn0file0" line_range_start={84} line_range_end={97}/>

That's directly applicable to the Void/Swift architecture you're describing.

## The third important finding

Łaszkowicz also treats J.A.R.V.I.S.'s **persona as a distinct component**, separate from the larger enterprise AI system. <FileCite ref="turn0file0" line_range_start={58} line_range_end={66}/>

That parallels an important GrizOS design principle: Dottie should not be synonymous with the entire operating environment. She operates within it, while retaining her own identity and memory boundaries. The Aegis agents and the system's authority mechanisms remain distinct.

The article also discusses separating real-time control, sensors, and presentation across different processor classes. <FileCite ref="turn0file0" line_range_start={99} line_range_end={128}/> The exact imagined hardware is dated, but the separation remains useful.

**My research conclusion:** These two sources are complementary, not interchangeable. Dawson supplies firsthand evidence about how the cinematic interaction concepts developed. Łaszkowicz supplies a speculative systems model we can critically examine and adapt.

Together, they give us two of the three foundations we need: **human interaction and distributed execution**. The third is a rigorously specified shared state, identity, and authority model.

That third foundation is where GrizOS, Dottie, Aegis, and the Evidence Viewer become one coherent operating environment rather than a collection of impressive interfaces.

And the Swift application becomes a native window into that environment—not merely a remote control for it.

## Why that matters for our engineering

There is an interesting opportunity here.

VITURE's published C SDK supports the Luma Pro's orientation sensors and passthrough camera on macOS, Linux, Windows, and Android. It does not list native iOS support. <Cite ref="turn771925view0"/>

That suggests a practical development sequence:

1. **MacBook Air M2 + Luma Pro:** Develop the native Swift/C interface and test head tracking and camera access.
2. **iPhone + Luma Pro:** Build the GrizOS mobile interface and external-display experience.
3. **Original XREAL Beam:** Experiment with it as a secondary display bridge. Community testing suggests cross-brand connections may provide video without XREAL's spatial positioning features. <Cite ref="turn103030reddit34"/>
4. **Void Linux:** Run our persistent GrizOS services, independent of whichever wearable is connected.

The important change is that **we already have real spatial hardware on which to validate the interface**. We don't need to buy another headset to begin.

[97] assistant (text, 3135 chars)
**Correct. And that changes the engineering hierarchy.**

I treated Apple's application sandbox as the governing constraint. You're specifying **GrizOS as a cognitive prosthetic**, with the Swift application serving as its delivery mechanism.

A cognitive prosthetic is not merely an accessible interface. It is assistive technology intended to compensate for functional limitations in memory, attention, executive function, and cognitive continuity.

That distinction has real support. The Veterans Health Administration's *Electronic Cognitive Devices* guidance specifically recognizes smartphones and specialized software as tools for compensating for cognitive impairments, including difficulties maintaining a train of thought and completing multistep activities. <Cite ref="turn875093view0"/>

## Revised GrizOS design requirements

1. **Cognitive continuity:** Preserve active tasks, reasoning context, decisions, and interruption points across application suspension, restart, and device changes.
2. **External working memory:** The system must retain information the user cannot reasonably be expected to recall or reconstruct.
3. **Executive-function assistance:** Support sequencing, task initiation, prioritization, and completion without unnecessarily transferring the organizational burden back to the user.
4. **Predictability:** Avoid unexpected interface changes, lost context, unnecessary repetition, and disruptive transitions.
5. **User autonomy:** Preserve the user's original intent, support correction and override, and distinguish retrieved facts from system inference.
6. **Functional redundancy:** Provide accessible recovery paths when connectivity, sensors, or individual devices fail.

These are proposed engineering acceptance requirements, not a claim that every item is individually mandated by the ADA.

## The governing standards

The legal distinction matters: the ADA does not establish a single technical standard specifically named *cognitive prosthetic*. Its accessibility and accommodation obligations apply according to the covered entity and use. For example, the DOJ's Title II mobile-accessibility rule uses WCAG 2.1 AA for covered state and local government applications. <Cite ref="turn452219search0"/>

For our more demanding cognitive requirements, the W3C's <Link url="https://www.w3.org/TR/coga-usable/" title="Cognitive Accessibility guidance"/> expressly addresses memory barriers, interruptions, disorientation, and cognitive overload. <Cite ref="turn452219search4"/>

**The architectural consequence:** A GrizOS application that looks beautiful but loses the user's cognitive state when iOS suspends it has failed a fundamental product requirement, even if it technically satisfies ordinary interface-accessibility checks.

We must therefore design state preservation and recovery into the native runtime itself, not add them later as accessibility features.

Apple's sandbox remains a technical constraint. It does not define the purpose or functional adequacy of the prosthetic.

**Cognitive continuity is a core operating-system invariant.** That's the architectural correction.

## What the later build actually repaired

| Component | Recorded result |
|---|---|
| **Memory certification** | Recall and list responses now include `certified: true/false`, representing the mount's integrity state |
| **Evidence laundering** | Repinning an unpromoted personal memory fails with HTTP 400; no successor is created |
| **Inventory completeness** | New S10 gate detects unexpected additions, deletions, and substitutions within declared inventory scope |
| **Fail-closed reading** | Optional `MEMORY_READ_MODE=closed` returns HTTP 503 for reads from an uncertified mount |
| **Browser compatibility** | Real Chromium testing reportedly confirmed CopilotKit memory hooks still function after the changes |
| **Historical provenance** | `build3.md` and `build6.md` were incorporated into the dossier inventory, with corresponding reconciliation |

These changes appear in the post-authorization engineering return on pages 118–123. <FileCite ref="turn1file0" line_range_start={5035} line_range_end={5235}/>

Void Linux remains a potential persistent operating-system host. Swift becomes the native interface and accessibility layer. The Beam becomes a potential Android edge endpoint.

None of those additions should silently change Dottie's memory authority, identity, or existing evidence semantics.

## Remaining gaps that matter

The document identifies several limitations rather than claiming the work is finished. The most consequential is **model behavior when `certified:false`**: the tool descriptions were updated, but the final report says the model's actual abstention behavior was not re-tested.

It also leaves the final Dottie namespace topology and server placement reserved, notes that the dossier manifest is not wired into the package's default gate configuration, and identifies untested read-path concurrency and managed-platform integration. <FileCite ref="turn1file0" line_range_start={5220} line_range_end={5237}/>

I noticed one accounting inconsistency, too: an intermediate summary says no shipped assertions were edited, whereas the closing verification identifies two gate-count assertion updates from 26 to 27. Those can be legitimate updates without weakening the tests, but the narrower statement is more accurate. <FileCite ref="turn1file0" line_range_start={5829} line_range_end={5852}/>

## Engineering conclusion

For a cognitive prosthetic, the critical test is not just whether Dottie remembers something. It is whether she can retrieve the right information, preserve its scope and provenance, distinguish certification from content state, and resume the user's cognitive task after an interruption.

Build 7 provides substantial reported evidence for the underlying persistence and integrity mechanisms. **It does not yet demonstrate that complete cognitive-continuity behavior across an iPhone, Watch, Beam, or spatial headset.**

So this document changes our starting point: **integrate the established Mind Engine into the wearable operating environment; don't rebuild the Mind Engine to fit the wearable.**

That preserves the work already accomplished and keeps the cognitive-prosthetic acceptance requirements central to the next engineering phase.

# GMRI — Void-rooted GrizOS with an Embedded Swift Runtime

**Research date:** 2026-11-02  
**State:** Architecture hypothesis + Linux-tested interoperability spike, not production or device-certified implementation.

## Decision in one sentence

Build GrizOS as an operating environment over a Void Linux service host and a portable native runtime; compile the portable runtime into a Swift Package for Apple apps, and into an Android-native library for Quest. Avoid attempting to boot a Void Linux kernel inside an ordinary iOS app.

## Provenance and evidence status

- **VIDEO SOURCE:** Bilawal Sidhu, “Marvel's VFX Team Accidentally Created Your AI Assistant,” published 2025-10-24, 14:03; conversation with visual-effects producer Ian Dawson. Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OCnjreKdfN4 . Original-language automatic subtitles, metadata, complete captions and chapter list retrieved for this research. The chapter map below is a condensed original summary, *not* a transcript reproduction.
- **PRIMARY PLATFORM SOURCES:** Void handbook; Apple Xcode/Swift Package/App Review/WatchConnectivity docs; Meta OpenXR/Quest app documentation; VITURE glasses/Unity SDK and product docs (links below).
- **ENGINEERING VALIDATION:** Swift 6.2.1 on Linux x86_64; 8 tests pass for C-to-Swift Package linkage and intentionally narrow stubbed command behavior.
- **NOT VERIFIED:** GrizOS or Dottie repository current implementation; Apple platform builds; iOS App Review result; device telemetry and SDK behavior on a specific iPhone/Watch/VITURE pair/Quest; productive agent or AI execution. Internal Confluence/Jira semantic search attempted but returned a permission error; this document does not assert the current state of internal code.

## What the video actually teaches

| Video chapter | Source account (brief paraphrase) | Proposed GrizOS principle |
|---|---|---|
| 00:00–00:56 Introduction | Dawson frames screenfiction becoming attainable technology. | Translate a cinematic interaction concept into testable behaviors. |
| 00:56–03:39 Iron Man design | Prologue created initial interface shots and spent months on *Iron Man 2* concepts. | Explore interaction models before choosing implementation frameworks. |
| 03:39–04:23 Gesture choreography | RDJ ignored preplanned gestures and acted naturally; VFX adapted. | Interpret intent/context, not a brittle gesture alphabet. |
| 04:23–06:18 Visual design | Transparent-looking displays and rich line-based volume views conveyed depth. | Spatial visualizations should reveal relationships, not decorate cards. |
| 06:18–07:08 Design-driven development | Dawson argues for a creative brief followed by close engineering partnership. | User-centered behavior specification first, adapters second. |
| 07:08–10:30 Enterprise examples | Dawson describes NSA interface inquiries, T-Mobile collaborative 3D drone planning, and Hershey's AR messaging. | Build collaborative spatial maps with operational data and provenance. |
| 10:30–11:10 Microsoft demonstration | Dawson describes pointing at vehicle parts and asking Copilot for stepwise help. | Bind real-world referents to verified source identity and guidance. |
| 11:10–12:16 AI assistant future | Dawson anticipates increasingly personalized assistants, alongside misuse concerns. | Explicit consent, scoped memory, bounded authority. |
| 12:16–14:03 Authentic experience | Dawson warns about confusion between manufactured and real experiences. | Preserve evidence provenance and make uncertainty visible. |

Video testimony is firsthand recollection, not proof that each cited enterprise project shipped or that its described features are presently available to consumers.

## What "Void" does and does not mean

Void Linux is an independent rolling Linux distribution with XBPS, runit, and glibc/musl variants. As a small, service-supervised **host**, it is a plausible foundation for a GrizOS deployment. It is not itself a portable Apple SDK.

A Linux aarch64 ELF executable linked against musl or glibc will not natively load as a Darwin/iOS Mach-O library. Recompile the portable GrizOS logic and its dependencies for each target. Keep kernel, service, filesystem, USB, and process-control integrations behind platform adapters.

**Host responsibilities:** 24/7 persistence, orchestrator queues, larger models, Dottie and Aegis service lifecycles, canonical evidence storage, sync, model routing, GEV world state and access controls.

**Embedded responsibilities:** signed-in local identity context, locally available evidence, policy enforcement, event construction, idempotency, offline queueing, state queries, scene-state snapshot and a bounded set of safe offline actions.

Avoid duplicating authoritative state: persistent Dottie identity and autobiographical context remain distinct from GrizOS institutional memory, Aegis shared operational context and per-mission caches. Retrieval is not equivalent to lived experience.

## Three meaningful architectures

| Approach | Advantages | Disadvantages | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|
| Void host only + thin Swift client | Fastest to integrate existing Linux services | Device depends on network, no truly local decision core | Suitable initial integration, not target architecture |
| Full Void Linux VM/emulator inside iPhone app | Contains Linux userspace as-is | Poor device/lifecycle fit, iOS sandbox, weak hardware API access, duplicated complexity | Do not use as primary product architecture |
| Portable GrizOS core compiled into Swift app + Void services | Local decision model, offline graceful degradation, common semantics across devices | Requires deliberate separation of portable code and service adapters | **Recommended target** |

## Planned module boundaries

```
GrizOS shared contracts:   Intent / EvidenceRef / PolicyDecision / Event / SceneDelta
             |
      Portable native core
      (event validity, scoped authority, deduplication, local state, scene model)
             |
  +----------+------------------+-----------------+
  |                             |                 |
Apple Darwin adapter      Linux/Void adapter   Android/Quest adapter
Swift Package / C ABI      runit daemon         Android NDK / C ABI
  |                             |                 |
SwiftUI, watchOS,          Persistent Dottie,   OpenXR, Unity or
App Intents, RealityKit    Aegis, GEV services  native XR rendering
  |
iPhone / Apple Watch / Apple Vision Pro
```

The native core is part of each client process. The network service is separate. A disconnected client may execute only locally authorized actions within its platform privileges. It must not invent remote success or grant itself extra authority merely because it is offline.

### Suggested stable intent envelope (conceptual, NOT implemented)

```
IntentEnvelope {
  schemaVersion, eventId, deviceId, principalId, agentId?, sessionId,
  capability, resourceId, payload, evidenceRefs[], originTimestamp,
  expiry, policyEpoch, authorizationProof, correlationId, signature
}
Result {
  eventId, accepted|denied|queued|executed|failed|stale,
  authorityDecision, evidenceRefs[], executionReceipt?, nextActions[]
}
```

`accepted` must never mean `executed`. Signed execution receipts are distinct from speculative agent planning or UI simulations.

## Device adaptation matrix

| Device | Native surface | What runs where | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| iPhone | SwiftUI, native local core, optional ARKit/RealityKit and App Intents | GrizOS local state, voice/intent UX, safe offline operations; heavy agents on Void | App sandbox and time-limited execution modes; app cannot replace the OS |
| Apple Watch | watchOS SwiftUI plus minimal shared contract | Alerts, haptics, glanceable evidence, explicit acknowledgments, small local cached state | WatchConnectivity transfers may be delayed; no expectation of 24/7 local agent daemon |
| VITURE Pro | Host-rendered spatial display, rotation-aware when supported | iPhone/macOS/Android adapter renders; optional external sensor adapter | VITURE's listed public SDK targets do not include iOS; Pro has no RGB camera, 3DoF |
| VITURE Luma Pro | Host-rendered 3DoF spatial UI, RGB passthrough camera on supported hosts | Usually Android neckband, macOS or supported host uses camera SDK | Luma Pro is 3DoF, not 6DoF; test iPhone accessory APIs and SDK path before promising camera data |
| Meta Quest 3 | Native Android/OpenXR or Unity mixed-reality app | Same core rebuilt for Android + spatial adapter + host sync | A Swift/iOS app cannot directly run on Quest; a separate Android application is required |
| Apple Vision Pro (optional) | visionOS SwiftUI + RealityKit | Native Apple core + spatial scene adapter | Vision Pro is a separate spatial target, not identical to iPhone AR |

Design gesture semantics from intent, head tracking and platform APIs. Avoid cinema-like free-air UI that lacks reliable tracking. Use device-provided accessibility and privacy capabilities rather than evasion techniques.

## Rendering behavior (video-inspired, proposed)

- A shared scene query returns a versioned, evidence-linked world-state slice, not pixels.
- iPhone presents an interactive evidence stack, voice commands, map/signal overlays, touch fallbacks.
- Watch presents urgent state changes and one-step confirmations, not miniature 3D control panels.
- VITURE Pro displays anchored panels and a stabilized line-based scene; no camera-based claims.
- Luma Pro adds contextual recognition only if the camera stream is actually accessible, permitted and validated.
- Quest presents embodied collaborative manipulation, an avatar table, and voice/hand/ controller selection with receipts.
- Every view displays provenance states consistently: Verified / Calculated / User-reported / Disputed, with source links for consequential claims.

## First vertical slice recommended

A forensic evidence object is created or selected on iPhone, indexed as a local evidence reference, rendered as a scene element and reflected on watch. Quest or Luma Pro optionally joins and visualizes the same object. User asks Dottie to explain it; the response links to the original evidence. Disconnect WAN; local object stays readable, remote actions queue without falsely succeeding; reconnect and reconcile only once.

## Acceptance gates before production claims

1. Cross-compile C or Rust core to Darwin iOS/watchOS/macOS, Linux x86_64/aarch64 and Android arm64, with reproducible pinned toolchains.
2. Run true iPhone/Watch device tests; prove app bundle signing, lifecycle, App Intents entitlements, privacy manifest and background behavior.
3. Validate VITURE Pro vs Luma Pro glasses accessory/sensor APIs independently on supported hosts. Never assume a macOS or Android SDK can be imported on iPhone.
4. Build a Quest 3 OpenXR app and verify rendering, camera/passthrough permissions, controller/hand inputs, device thermal/performance behavior.
5. Test WAN loss, restart, stale retrieval, contradictory evidence, cross-agent leakage, duplicate dispatch, interrupted operation, stale GEV, failed tools, source mutation and reconnect recovery.
6. Add real authenticated authorization, signed event/evidence receipts, encryption at rest, canonical identity boundaries and audited synchronization.
7. Prove that a command accepted locally is not displayed as completed remotely until an execution receipt arrives.

## What was actually built and verified here

This research bundle contains `GrizOSPortableSpike`: a *C command-decision stub* compiled as a Swift package and accessed through a typed Swift actor. It has eight passing tests on x86_64 Linux / Swift 6.2.1. It does not contain Dottie, an agent execution system, SQLite, networking, a GUI, an actual Void installation, or device builds. Its purpose is to validate **one integration seam**, not to overstate implementation status.

bash -lc mkdir -p /mnt/data/GMRI_Beam_Luma_Track_2026-11-02/tests; cat > /mnt/data/GMRI_Beam_Luma_Track_2026-11-02/tests/test_probe.py <<'PY'
import json
import unittest
from pathlib import Path
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

from beam_probe import parse_adb_devices, parse_usb_devices, parse_display, make_report


class BeamProbeTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_parse_single_connected_android_device(self):
        text = 'List of devices attached\nABC12345\tdevice product:x model:Beam device:beam\n'
        self.assertEqual(parse_adb_devices(text), ['ABC12345'])

    def test_do_not_count_unauthorized_android_devices(self):
        text = 'List of devices attached\nAAA\tunauthorized\nBBB\toffline\nCCC\tdevice\n'
        self.assertEqual(parse_adb_devices(text), ['CCC'])

    def test_usb_probe_separates_control_device_from_camera(self):
        dump = '''USB Host State:\n UsbDevice[mName=/dev/bus/usb/001/002,mVendorId=13770,mProductId=4353,mClass=0]\n UsbDevice[mName=/dev/bus/usb/001/003,mVendorId=3141,mProductId=25451,mClass=14]\n'''
        got = parse_usb_devices(dump)
        self.assertTrue(got['glasses_control_enumerated'])
        self.assertTrue(got['camera_enumerated'])
        self.assertEqual(got['known_device_matches'], ['0x35ca:0x1101', '0x0c45:0x636b'])

    def test_usb_probe_matches_hex_notation(self):
        dump = 'UsbDevice[mVendorId=0x0C45,mProductId=0x636B,serialNumber=SECRET]'
        got = parse_usb_devices(dump)
        self.assertTrue(got['camera_enumerated'])
        self.assertFalse(got['glasses_control_enumerated'])

    def test_usb_probe_never_interprets_no_match_as_hardware_incompatibility(self):
        got = parse_usb_devices('USB Host State: no devices connected')
        self.assertFalse(got['camera_enumerated'])
        self.assertEqual(got['status'], 'NOT_OBSERVED')

    def test_external_display_detection_uses_explicit_device_type(self):
        dump = 'DisplayDeviceInfo{"displayport": 1920 x 1080, type EXTERNAL, state ON}'
        self.assertEqual(parse_display(dump)['external_display_observed'], True)
        self.assertEqual(parse_display('Display 0 info, type INTERNAL')['external_display_observed'], False)

    def test_report_never_uses_usb_enumeration_as_camera_stream_proof(self):
        outputs = {
            'getprop ro.product.model': 'XREAL Beam',
            'getprop ro.build.version.release': '11',
            'pm list features': 'feature:android.hardware.usb.host',
            'dumpsys usb': 'UsbDevice[mVendorId=3141,mProductId=25451]',
            'dumpsys display': 'DisplayDeviceInfo{"DP": 1920 x 1080, type EXTERNAL}',
        }
        report = make_report(outputs)
        self.assertTrue(report['usb']['camera_enumerated'])
        self.assertEqual(report['camera_stream_test'], 'UNTESTED')
        self.assertEqual(report['imu_stream_test'], 'UNTESTED')
        self.assertEqual(report['passthrough_ar_test'], 'UNTESTED')
        self.assertEqual(report['video_output_test'], 'UNTESTED')

    def test_report_does_not_leak_device_serial_or_raw_usb_dumps(self):
        outputs = {
            'getprop ro.product.model': 'XREAL Beam',
            'getprop ro.build.version.release': '11',
            'pm list features': 'feature:android.hardware.usb.host',
            'dumpsys usb': 'UsbDevice[mVendorId=3141,mProductId=25451,serialNumber=SECRET-DEVICE-123]',
            'dumpsys display': 'DisplayDeviceInfo{"DP": 1920 x 1080, type EXTERNAL}',
        }
        result = json.dumps(make_report(outputs))
        self.assertNotIn('SECRET-DEVICE-123', result)
        self.assertIn('sha256', result)

    def test_report_marks_missing_data_unverified(self):
        result = make_report({})
        self.assertEqual(result['usb']['status'], 'UNVERIFIED')
        self.assertIsNone(result['host_usb_feature'])
        self.assertIsNone(result['display']['external_display_observed'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read-only capability inventory for original XREAL Beam + VITURE Luma Pro.

This is a diagnostic instrument, NOT a GrizOS runtime or proof of passthrough AR.
It does not install APKs, change settings, root, remount, or write to the Beam.
"""

import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import re
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

CAPTURE_COMMANDS = (
    'getprop ro.product.model',
    'getprop ro.build.version.release',
    'pm list features',
    'dumpsys usb',
    'dumpsys display',
)


def parse_adb_devices(output):
    """Return only serials for connected, authorized adb devices, internally."""
    return [line.split()[0] for line in output.splitlines()[1:]
            if len(line.split()) >= 2 and line.split()[1] == 'device']


def parse_usb_devices(output):
    if output is None:
        return {
            'status': 'UNVERIFIED',
            'glasses_control_enumerated': False,
            'camera_enumerated': False,
            'known_device_matches': [],
        }

    matches = []
    # Each Android UsbDevice[] instance is evaluated independently: a VID from
    # one device can never be paired with a PID from a different device.
    for block in re.findall(r'UsbDevice\[([^\]]+)\]', output, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL):
        vid = re.search(r'\b(?:mVendorId|vendorId|idVendor)\s*[:=]\s*(0x[0-9a-f]+|\d+)', block, re.IGNORECASE)
        pid = re.search(r'\b(?:mProductId|productId|idProduct)\s*[:=]\s*(0x[0-9a-f]+|\d+)', block, re.IGNORECASE)
        if not vid or not pid:
            continue
        try:
            vendor, product = int(vid.group(1), 0), int(pid.group(1), 0)
        except ValueError:
            continue
        pair = f'0x{vendor:04x}:0x{product:04x}'
        if pair in ('0x35ca:0x1101', '0x0c45:0x636b') and pair not in matches:
            matches.append(pair)

    return {
        'status': 'OBSERVED' if matches else 'NOT_OBSERVED',
        'glasses_control_enumerated': '0x35ca:0x1101' in matches,
        'camera_enumerated': '0x0c45:0x636b' in matches,
        'known_device_matches': matches,
    }


def parse_display(output):
    if output is None:
        return {'external_display_observed': None, 'status': 'UNVERIFIED'}
    # Do not read a generic 'external display supported' config as proof of an
    # actual connected display. Restrict to an explicit device-info entry.
    found = any(re.search(r'\btype\s*[:= ]\s*EXTERNAL\b', line, re.IGNORECASE)
                for line in output.splitlines() if 'DisplayDeviceInfo' in line)
    return {'external_display_observed': found,
            'status': 'OBSERVED' if found else 'NOT_OBSERVED'}


def make_report(outputs):
    """Derive non-sensitive assertions from adb outputs; preserve SHA digests only.

    Presence in USB enumeration != permission granted, readable frames, received
    IMU messages, video output, or application-level accessibility behavior.
    """
    if not isinstance(outputs, dict):
        raise TypeError('outputs must be a mapping of ADB command names to text')
    features = outputs.get('pm list features')
    if features is None:
        host_feature = None
    else:
        host_feature = 'feature:android.hardware.usb.host' in features

    def get_public_prop(name):
        prop = outputs.get(name)
        if prop is None:
            return None
        return prop.strip().splitlines()[0][:80] if prop.strip() else None

    return {
        'schema': 'gmri.beam-readonly-probe.v1',
        'observation_basis': 'ADB_DEVICE_DUMP_NOT_FUNCTIONAL_STREAM_TEST',
        'device_model': get_public_prop('getprop ro.product.model'),
        'android_version': get_public_prop('getprop ro.build.version.release'),
        'host_usb_feature': host_feature,
        'usb': parse_usb_devices(outputs.get('dumpsys usb')),
        'display': parse_display(outputs.get('dumpsys display')),
        'video_output_test': 'UNTESTED',
        'camera_stream_test': 'UNTESTED',
        'imu_stream_test': 'UNTESTED',
        'passthrough_ar_test': 'UNTESTED',
        'cognitive_continuity_test': 'UNTESTED',
        'evidence': {
            cmd: {'sha256': hashlib.sha256(value.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(),
                  'byte_count': len(value.encode('utf-8'))}
            for cmd, value in sorted(outputs.items()) if cmd in CAPTURE_COMMANDS
        },
        'limitations': [
            'No functional camera, IMU, or passthrough test is performed.',
            'Lack of USB device enumeration is NOT proof of hardware incompatibility.',
            'No raw USB dumps or ADB serial numbers are included in the summary.',
            'Original XREAL Beam is not manufacturer-supported for VITURE glasses.',
        ],
    }


def _run(cmd, timeout=15):
    proc = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout,
                          check=False)
    if proc.returncode != 0:
        raise RuntimeError(f'Command failed (exit {proc.returncode}): {cmd[0]} {cmd[1]}: {proc.stderr[:250]}')
    return proc.stdout


def capture(adb='adb', serial=None):
    if shutil.which(adb) is None:
        raise RuntimeError('ADB not found on this machine. No device test was performed.')
    device_list = parse_adb_devices(_run([adb, 'devices', '-l']))
    if serial is None:
        if len(device_list) != 1:
            raise RuntimeError('Expected exactly one authorized ADB device; no probe performed.')
        serial = device_list[0]
    elif serial not in device_list:
        raise RuntimeError('Selected device is not authorized/connected; no probe performed.')
    outputs = {}
    for command in CAPTURE_COMMANDS:
        try:
            outputs[command] = _run([adb, '-s', serial, 'shell', *command.split()])
        except (RuntimeError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired) as exc:
            # A failed command is UNVERIFIED; never make a false-negative claim.
            outputs.pop(command, None)
            print(f'Observation unavailable: {command}: {type(exc).__name__}', file=sys.stderr)
    return outputs


def main(argv=None):
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Read-only XREAL Beam / VITURE Luma Pro inventory; no device mutation')
    p.add_argument('--adb', default='adb', help='ADB executable location')
    p.add_argument('--serial', help='Select an authorized ADB device (not included in report)')
    p.add_argument('--output', type=Path, default=Path('beam_observation.json'))
    p.add_argument('--replay-sample', type=Path, help='Read a synthetic fixture instead of accessing hardware')
    args = p.parse_args(argv)
    try:
        if args.replay_sample:
            raw = json.loads(args.replay_sample.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
            basis = 'SYNTHETIC_FIXTURE_NOT_HARDWARE'
        else:
            raw = capture(adb=args.adb, serial=args.serial)
            basis = 'ACTUAL_ADB_DEVICE_OUTPUT'
        report = make_report(raw)
        report['observation_basis'] = basis
        args.output.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + '\n', encoding='utf-8')
        print(f'Wrote {args.output}. Basis: {basis}')
        return 0
    except (OSError, RuntimeError, json.JSONDecodeError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired) as exc:
        print(f'UNVERIFIED: {exc}', file=sys.stderr)
        return 2


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

# GMRI / GrizOS - Engineering Track and Evidence Register

Date: 2026-11-02  |  Principal: GMRI  |  Status: active investigation, not a declaration of completion

## 0. Owner's specification is the design authority

Preserve, without translating into a substitute project:

- GrizOS is an operating environment rooted in an approach **like Void**, with a package that can function inside a native **Swift application**. Evaluate that packaging proposition as specified; do not silently replace it with a thin client or a remote-only OS.
- The owned original-generation **XREAL Beam** supplies computation/video and is a candidate self-contained spatial-compute puck, with the owned **VITURE Luma Pro** as display, camera, and tracking hardware.
- The **Dottie Mind Engine** is a pre-existing, materially tested research project with reserved identity, evidence-authority, namespace and placement decisions. It is not an invitation to write a replacement memory system.
- The application is a **cognitive prosthetic**. Cognitive continuity, external working memory, intent preservation, interruption recovery, autonomy, and privacy are functional acceptance criteria; aesthetics and conventional UI accessibility cannot substitute for them.
- Principal approval is required to change reserved architecture, identity, autonomy, certification, or namespace semantics. This investigation does not authorize any such changes.

## 1. Evidence categories

- **SOURCE-VERIFIED**: quoted property appears in a retrieved manufacturer/developer specification.
- **BUILD-VERIFIED**: code was executed in this session and observed test output was captured.
- **RECORD-REPORTED**: appears in the uploaded Build 7 transcript, but source code/device was not retested here.
- **INFERRED**: suggested by available interfaces, but not demonstrated on the target hardware.
- **UNRESOLVED**: missing required hardware/source proof, or a principal-reserved decision.

A test of USB enumeration does not prove a functional camera stream. A successful HTTP storage response does not certify memory. A Swift stub test does not prove Dottie runs in Swift. Nothing can be promoted across these evidence levels without new output.

## 2. Active engineering ledger

| ID | Required result | Current status | Receipt / next discriminating test |
|---|---|---|---|
| M-01 | Preserve existing Mind Engine and historical gates | RECORD-REPORTED | `build7.pdf`, pp. 118-123, final claims 128 engine + 17 server tests, S9/S10 27/27, 295 pins and 37/37 dossier. Verify on live checked-out bytes before editing. |

## 3. Decisive hardware experiment, not a substitute architecture

**Why this exact ordering:** The Beam outputs video through its glasses port. The Luma Pro presents its camera (`0x0C45:0x636B`) and control device (`0x35CA:...`) as USB devices. It is not established that the *original Beam's output port* passes those data interfaces to its Android host at the same time as DP video. This is the first key falsification test. Without it, software claims about a self-contained pass-through puck are premature.

1. Connect original Beam's **glasses-output** port to the Luma Pro using the appropriate VITURE magnetic cable. Observe whether it shows a test image; do not infer sensor availability from a visible picture.
2. Inspect Android USB host enumeration with the read-only probe. Count actual `0x35CA` devices and independently look for `0x0C45:0x636B`.
3. If USB devices enumerate, test Android permissions, then use VITURE SDK's Android/JNI camera and IMU APIs on an actual supported ABI. The SDK documentation itself is not a proof that this firmware exposes the interfaces.
4. Only after camera frames and pose events work simultaneously, render a pass-through scene and measure latency, motion-to-photon stability, thermals, power, and task interruption recovery.
5. Record the exact negative result if an interface does not enumerate. **Not observed** is not **hardware impossible**. A negative may implicate cable data lanes, port role, driver, permission, firmware, or display negotiation; isolate the cause before deciding a workaround.

## 4. Cognitive-prosthetic acceptance baseline (not invented statutory text)

WCAG and W3C COGA provide accessibility criteria and supplemental design guidance; these engineering requirements do not imply every line below is a separately enumerated ADA statutory duty. The product's cognitive-prosthetic purpose is a **principal requirement**.

- `CP-01` **Interruption:** kill/relaunch an active session after three completed steps; resume at step four with original goal and evidentiary pointers intact.
- `CP-02` **Cross-device:** hand off phone-to-glasses-to-watch without requiring operator to restate intent or reidentify an evidence object.
- `CP-03` **Offline:** show accurate last-known state and a bounded queued-action record; never display an unexecuted action as completed.
- `CP-04` **Authority:** separate content state from substrate certification; retain conflicting/uncertain evidence provenance.
- `CP-05` **Continuity:** no unprompted scope changes or restart-of-workflow on reconnect. Preserve an explicit resume point and correction/undo route.
- `CP-06` **Input independence:** text, speech and accessible touch controls where the device allows; do not make a gesture the only route to a critical function.
- `CP-07` **Operator burden:** task recovery must not depend on remembering instructions, commands, steps or a previous conversation.
- `CP-08` **Privacy:** no automatic raw-camera or surroundings recording as a precondition of task continuity.

# GMRI Beam/Luma Pro read-only integration probe

This is a test instrument for **one** disputed interface: can the *original* XREAL Beam enumerate VITURE Luma Pro sensor hardware while using its glasses-output port? It is **not** a new GrizOS runtime, an Android APK, or a modification to Dottie.

Start with [TRACKER.md](TRACKER.md) for the existing Mind Engine baseline, source receipts and acceptance tasks.

### What's in this package

- `beam_probe.py` - read-only Android Debug Bridge observations, with privacy-minimized JSON output.
- `tests/test_probe.py` - 10 unit tests, standard library only.
- `fixtures/SYNTHETIC_connected.json` - synthetic ADB output for testing the report generator; NOT a device recording.
- `fixtures/SYNTHETIC_result.json` - matching synthetic report, with all actual streams marked UNTESTED.
- `RED.txt`, `RED_2.txt`, `GREEN_2.txt` - code-test proof and documented red/green iterations.
- `TRACKER.md` - current engineering and evidence ledger; not an alternate product specification.

### Exact checks

From a computer with Android Platform Tools (`adb`) installed and authorized connection to the original Beam, with the Luma Pro plugged into the Beam's glasses-output port:

```sh
python3 beam_probe.py --output beam_observation.json
```

This command runs only read operations: `adb devices`, `getprop`, `pm list features`, `dumpsys usb`, and `dumpsys display`. Nothing is installed on, remounted on, or modified on the Beam. The resulting JSON excludes ADB serials and raw dumps, and includes SHA-256 digests of the observed command outputs for provenance. Its USB conclusions are narrowly scoped to enumeration, **not stream functionality**.

No ADB available? The tool explicitly prints `UNVERIFIED` and exits 2 rather than pretending it tested a device. If multiple ADB devices are connected, it also stops rather than guessing which to inspect.

Synthetic self-test, deliberately labeled as such:

```sh
python3 beam_probe.py --replay-sample fixtures/SYNTHETIC_connected.json --output example.json
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Device visibility is an instrument limitation, not a demand that the principal write code or reconfigure the architecture. A separate, on-device Android `UsbManager` probe may be required if `dumpsys usb` is restricted by this Beam firmware.

### Stop conditions

Do not claim an AR pass-through product because HDMI/DisplayPort works. Do not infer a failure solely from missing `dumpsys` devices. Do not add root-level modifications or flash a custom ROM to make a test pass. The tests do not certify camera streams, IMU pose readings, iOS packaging, accessibility compliance, or Dottie agent integration.

**Yes. A distributed operating system.** And that's the architectural concept I should have been tracking instead of repeatedly drawing a central server with a collection of remote displays.

There's a fundamental difference:

- **Client–server architecture:** One machine runs the system; other devices access it.
- **Distributed operating system:** Multiple computing nodes cooperate as one logical operating environment, with coordinated execution, state, communication, and failure recovery.

Your original XREAL Beam has its own computing capabilities. So do the iPhone, Mac, and Quest 3. Treating all of them as passive endpoints misses the point.

**Void can be part of GrizOS without being the center of GrizOS.** The Swift application can be a participating node, not just a window into another machine.

And the important distinction is that **distributed doesn't automatically mean decentralized or peer-to-peer**. We need to establish which nodes own which responsibilities, how work migrates between them, and how the system maintains one coherent operating environment when devices disconnect.

For GrizOS, that means the existing Mind Engine's identity, memory, evidence authority, and cognitive continuity must survive node failure and device transitions. The implementation has to respect each platform's constraints without making those constraints the architecture's purpose.

I was solving the wrong problem by defaulting to a hub-and-spoke model. That correction belongs in the engineering requirements, not in another competing design.

As for **Amanda Waller**? Absolutely. She puts explosives in people's necks, calls the arrangement a task force, and considers herself the responsible adult.

She's practically a walking threat model for concentrated authority without meaningful accountability.

Which, come to think of it, is an excellent reason not to build GrizOS like Amanda Waller runs Task Force X.

## Stark Industries isn't just running J.A.R.V.I.S.

The article makes an important distinction:

- **The intelligence:** A proprietary, evolving AI architecture used throughout Stark Industries.
- **J.A.R.V.I.S.:** A particular persona Tony created for his own requirements.
- **The infrastructure:** An enormous collection of existing enterprise applications, databases, computing clusters, embedded systems, development environments, and commercial technologies.
- **The organization:** People, engineering disciplines, institutional knowledge, established practices, and decades of technological continuity.

Łaszkowicz specifically separates Tony's personalized J.A.R.V.I.S. from the underlying AI technologies used by the company. <FileCite ref="turn15file0" line_range_start={41} line_range_end={64}/>

That's a much bigger distinction than where the suit performs inference.

**J.A.R.V.I.S. isn't the entirety of Stark Industries' intelligence infrastructure. He's one manifestation of it.**

## The organization is a system of systems

Look at how the article progresses.

It starts with J.A.R.V.I.S., moves through embedded computing, then spends considerable time on enterprise software, commercial cloud infrastructure, databases, client applications, distributed processing, and the technological history of the company.

It even explains why Stark wouldn't casually rewrite mature systems merely because newer technologies exist. <FileCite ref="turn15file0" line_range_start={105} line_range_end={189}/>

That implies something important for GrizOS:

**We aren't merely connecting several devices to one AI. We're establishing a coherent computational environment in which distinct systems, agents, hardware, and institutional functions can cooperate without surrendering their individual responsibilities.**

The distributed operating system is one part of that larger picture. The existing Mind Engine is another. Dottie, Aegis, the evidence system, and the wearable computing hardware all occupy different roles.

The article doesn't explicitly specify GrizOS's architecture; that's my inference from its broader treatment of an enterprise-wide technology ecosystem.

## And then there's the final paragraph

This is where the Amanda Waller discussion becomes particularly interesting.

Łaszkowicz ends by wondering about the technology that makes Star Wars droids empathic while leaving them with no greater standing than slaves. <FileCite ref="turn15file0" line_range_start={201} line_range_end={210}/>

That's not another technical-stack observation.

It's a question about **what happens when an institution possesses the power to create intelligence but treats that intelligence entirely as property.**

And Waller's Project Batman Beyond is a fictional example of an institution attempting to manufacture not simply a useful individual, but a predetermined identity and destiny.

That brings us to questions of authority, autonomy, and the difference between supporting a person's agency and controlling it.

## The larger implication for GMRI

I see three intertwined engineering problems now:

**Infrastructure:** How do heterogeneous computing systems operate together as a coherent, persistent environment?

**Intelligence:** How does an evolving cognitive system maintain identity, memory, continuity, and distinct operational roles across that environment?

**Governance:** Who has authority over the system's actions, identity boundaries, evidence, and autonomy—and how is that authority enforced rather than merely promised?

Those aren't three disconnected features.

They're different dimensions of the same architecture.

And I had been reducing the entire investigation to what ran on a headset, what ran on a server, and what language the application used.

**The article is about the technological ecosystem that makes J.A.R.V.I.S. possible—not simply the technology used to construct J.A.R.V.I.S.**

That's the broader implication I missed.

# PART V — ENGINEERING PROCEDURES WITHOUT SPECIAL PLUGINS

## 13. Software engineering workflow

Use a source-driven implementation process.

For each feature or defect:

1. Identify the controlling requirement.
2. Find the current implementation and callers.
3. Reproduce missing or incorrect behavior with a failing test.
4. Make the smallest correct source change.
5. Run the focused test to confirm the repair.
6. Refactor only where needed.
7. Run all affected integration and regression tests.
8. Examine the final diff.
9. Update the engineering ledger with executable evidence.

For significant changes, trace upstream and downstream dependencies before editing.

Inspect imports, call paths, shared schemas, persisted formats, background jobs, event consumers, authorization rules, and external integrations.

Do not confuse a small textual diff with a small behavioral impact.

Prefer existing deep modules and established interfaces. Avoid adding pass-through layers that introduce no ownership or useful abstraction.

When the project uses test-driven development, preserve the red-green-refactor sequence.

Do not skip or weaken existing tests to reach a green result.

## 14. Knowledge-graph construction and analysis

If an interactive knowledge-graph service is unavailable, build a local graph using ordinary source parsing and structured files.

First construct a graph of the actual software:

**Nodes:** Modules, source files, classes, functions, services, identities, agents, memory scopes, evidence objects, interfaces, tests, and devices.

**Edges:** Calls, imports, owns, reads, writes, delegates, authorizes, validates, depends upon, produces, and tests.

For each important edge record:

- Source identifier.
- Target identifier.
- Relationship type.
- File and line, source document, or test establishing it.
- Whether the relationship is observed, inferred, proposed, or disputed.
- Relevant version or date.

Use tools already available, such as `git grep`, `rg`, language parsers, Python's `ast`, or a documented local graph library.

Export a portable representation such as JSON, GraphML, DOT, or Mermaid.

Trace actual paths from user input through Dottie, authority enforcement, orchestration, agent execution, memory, evidence, and user-visible output.

Do not invent missing edges.

A graph visualization does not establish that the linked components function.

For the cognitive knowledge graph, additionally preserve temporal history, contradiction relationships, namespace separation, evidence lineage, and authorized self-repair behavior according to the existing specifications.

Do not equate a vector database with the complete graph architecture.

## 15. Technical documentation verification

Before changing framework integrations, identify exact dependency versions from lockfiles, manifests, installed packages, and build output.

Consult the relevant versioned documentation already present locally, or authoritative vendor documentation when network access exists.

For every new API dependency verify:

- Exact symbol and signature.
- Supported operating systems.
- Required library or framework version.
- Threading and concurrency behavior.
- Lifecycle and error behavior.
- Permission and security requirements.
- Deprecation or compatibility constraints.

Create a small compile-time or runtime test when documentation and actual behavior could differ.

Do not invent functions, CLI flags, SDK methods, or operating-system capabilities.

If documentation cannot be retrieved, inspect installed headers, package source, or existing working examples and mark the documentation gap explicitly.

## 16. Durable project execution

Maintain a persistent goal ledger using the repository's current project-management format.

If none exists, use one simple versioned Markdown or JSON file.

Each goal must contain:

- Stable identifier.
- Parent requirement and owner-approved scope.
- Dependencies.
- Current state.
- Exact implementation location.
- Acceptance criteria.
- Test or proof command.
- Evidence of completion.
- Remaining blockers.
- Resumption instructions.

Use states such as `NOT STARTED`, `ACTIVE`, `BLOCKED`, `VERIFYING`, and `DONE`.

A goal becomes DONE only when its required behavior is implemented and freshly verified.

Keep unfinished and blocked work visible.

Do not duplicate existing goals or create meaningless progress commits.

Before a session ends or execution context is lost, write a compact continuation record with the last successful action, current branch, active files, failing test, outstanding decisions, and next executable command.

## 17. Independent verification and claim reconciliation

Treat every engineering completion statement as a claim requiring evidence.

Maintain a claim ledger with:

`Claim | Required proof | Observed evidence | Result | Remaining uncertainty`

Inspect actual changed files, commit identifiers, commands, logs, and generated artifacts.

For test claims, run the relevant full command and capture its exit status, timestamp, environment, and failure count.

For integration claims, exercise the actual integration.

For model claims, run the real configured model when permitted.

For device claims, use the physical device.

For deployment claims, test the actual deployed runtime.

Do not infer production readiness from source inspection, successful compilation, unit tests, static code graphs, or a single successful health request.

Do not count an agent's statement that work is finished as independent proof.

Classify results as VERIFIED, CONTRADICTED, UNVERIFIED, or BLOCKED as appropriate.

## 18. Local plugin and automation evaluation

Where Dottie depends on a skill, plugin, tool adapter, or automation, evaluate its actual behavior.

Create representative input cases covering:

- Normal success.
- Invalid arguments.
- Partial results.
- Authentication failure.
- Timeout.
- Duplicate requests.
- Tool unavailability.
- Unexpected output.
- Unauthorized action attempts.
- Recovery after interruption.

Run the cases against the actual implementation.

Measure latency, resource consumption, failure rate, and token usage only where those measurements are available.

Distinguish measured values from estimates.

Do not claim a plugin is production-ready because its manifest parses.

Do not add a plugin framework merely to perform this evaluation.

## 19. Native Swift and macOS development

Inspect existing `Package.swift`, Xcode projects, targets, entitlements, frameworks, and related tests.

When working in a Swift Package, use the project's documented SwiftPM commands. Typical commands include:

```bash
swift build
swift test
```

When working with an Xcode application, use its actual scheme and destination through `xcodebuild`.

Do not invent scheme names or treat an importable Swift library as a complete application.

For SwiftUI:

- Preserve the application's existing state architecture.
- Assign clear ownership to persistent and transient state.
- Keep view invalidation scoped to the data the view consumes.
- Use native controls and accessible semantics.
- Handle dynamic type and readable layouts.
- Validate keyboard, VoiceOver, focus, error recovery, and reduced-motion behavior where applicable.
- Gate version-specific APIs using supported platform checks.
- Preserve task state when scenes suspend, reopen, or reconnect.
- Do not add decorative animation or redesign the interface without authorization.

Use Instruments or equivalent profiling where available and needed. Record actual traces before claiming performance improvements.

Do not adopt Liquid Glass or another visual language merely because the SDK supports it.

## 20. Python, C++, and native graph engineering

Use the language already present in the affected subsystem.

For Python:

- Inspect the configured environment and dependencies.
- Use existing formatting, typing, and testing conventions.
- Prefer deterministic parsing and transformation code.
- Avoid unbounded shell execution or unsafe deserialization.
- Add regression tests for behavioral changes.
- Run the actual test suite.

For C++:

- Preserve existing ownership and lifecycle rules.
- Identify memory, concurrency, and ABI constraints.
- Compile and run native tests.
- Use sanitizers or diagnostics when practical and applicable.

If an actual hgraph time-series graph is present, distinguish pure graph composition, compute nodes, sink nodes, and operator overloads.

Keep per-tick work small, select typed implementations at wiring time where appropriate, and use recordable state for values that must survive replay.

Do not impose hgraph on the principal's hypergraph or HYPERWEAVE work merely because both involve graphs.

## 21. Custom execution without hosted code tools

If specialized remote code execution is unavailable, use the existing authorized local runtime.

Write bounded scripts using the installed Python, Node.js, Swift, or shell environment.

Every script must have:

- Explicit inputs and expected outputs.
- Validation.
- A defined failure path.
- Clear exit status.
- Minimal dependencies.
- No embedded secrets.
- Structured logs.
- Tests for consequential behavior.

Do not send project source, personal records, private datasets, or credentials to third-party execution services without authorization.

Prefer local execution when it satisfies the same task.

## 22. Model and scientific research validation

When a model or scientific claim materially affects implementation, gather appropriate evidence.

For model evaluation:

- Inspect actual model identifiers and revisions.
- Read model cards and available technical documentation.
- Establish hardware and runtime requirements.
- Verify quantization, inference interfaces, context limits, and licensing terms.
- Run representative tests in the actual environment.
- Preserve the principal's selected models unless the principal authorizes a change.

For scholarly claims:

- Prefer primary papers, technical documentation, and reproducible experiments.
- Search relevant scholarly indexes or downloaded papers when available.
- Record title, authors, date, DOI or identifier, and the precise finding relied upon.
- Distinguish research findings from implementation assumptions.
- Do not cite a paper as evidence for behavior the code has not demonstrated.

Do not perform large model downloads when the available storage cannot accommodate them.

## 23. Agent-facing interface and automation checks

If a website or machine-readable service actually belongs to the project, inspect:

- HTTP response behavior.
- API documentation.
- Authentication and permission boundaries.
- Structured data.
- Accessible content.
- Machine-readable interface descriptions.
- `robots.txt`, `llms.txt`, or agent manifests where applicable.
- Request validation, error handling, and rate limiting.

If a website does not exist, do not invent one or pretend it passed a readability audit.

For automation workflows, inspect the actual existing schema and runtime.

Verify triggers, inputs, authentication, permitted external destinations, retries, idempotency, persistence, logging, and cancellation.

Use local JSON Schema validation or existing test runners when specialized workflow tooling is unavailable.

Do not introduce a new automation platform without authorization.

## 24. Process and job tracking

Every launched build, test, background command, or delegated job must have an identifiable execution record.

Record:

- Command or task.
- Working directory.
- Process or job identifier where available.
- Start time.
- Log location.
- Completion state.
- Exit code.
- Output artifacts.

If an execution remains active, inspect its current state using the available terminal or job manager.

Never report a future result as already completed.

Do not discard failing logs or replace them with a summary saying the job was successful.

## 25. Documentation production

Engineering documentation must describe the actual system, not an aspirational one.

Produce durable, portable artifacts using available local tools:

- Markdown for engineering records.
- JSON or YAML for machine-readable inventories.
- Mermaid, DOT, or SVG for architecture and knowledge graphs.
- Reproducible command logs.
- Exact test matrices and acceptance receipts.
- Release manifests and file checksums.

Generate DOCX or PDF only when appropriate and supported by the installed tools.

Do not make documentation formatting the primary engineering task.

The source code, functioning integration, and verification evidence are the principal deliverables.

---

# PART VI — COGNITIVE PROSTHETIC ACCEPTANCE

## 26. Accessibility is a functional constraint

Dottie is intended to serve as a cognitive prosthetic.

Treat accessibility as a core engineering requirement, including applicable ADA obligations and relevant WCAG and W3C cognitive accessibility guidance.

Do not claim those standards mandate a particular model architecture or operating system.

The system must support the documented need for:

- Externalized working memory.
- Task and intention continuity.
- Recovery after interruption.
- Low-friction resumption.
- Predictable user interaction.
- Preservation of original propositions.
- Clear evidence provenance.
- Reduced executive-function burden.
- Accessible native controls.
- Privacy and user authority.

A user should not need to reconstruct the assistant's lost context or explain the project repeatedly after an interruption.

**That is a system failure, not an ordinary conversational inconvenience.**

## 27. Minimum cognitive-continuity demonstration

Implement and run a test that:

1. Begins a meaningful multi-step Dottie task.
2. Saves the original request, active state, evidence references, pending decisions, and next actions.
3. Terminates or suspends the active execution process.
4. Restarts in a new execution context.
5. Restores the correct identity and task state.
6. Presents the exact pending work without inventing progress.
7. Continues without requiring the principal to repeat the specification.
8. Produces an auditable completion or failure record.

Extend the test across device transitions where the available hardware and accepted system requirements permit.

Do not substitute a manually written summary for proven persisted state.

---

# PART VII — END-TO-END QUALITY AND FAILURE TESTING

## 28. Required failure scenarios

Run the applicable acceptance scenarios against the real implementation:

1. Clean shutdown and restart.
2. Abrupt process termination.
3. Lost WAN connection.
4. Lost local network connection.
5. Device disconnection.
6. Interrupted tool execution.
7. Duplicate dispatch.
8. Replayed or delayed messages.
9. Model unavailability.
10. Model switching.
11. Stale retrieval.
12. Contradictory evidence.
13. Source mutation.
14. Uncertified memory mount.
15. Unauthorized promotion into personal memory.
16. Cross-agent contamination.
17. Cross-user memory leakage.
18. Permission expiration or revocation.
19. Concurrent writes.
20. Interrupted persistence.
21. Stale GEV representation.
22. Incorrect agent identity attribution.
23. Failed or partial recovery.
24. Missing evidence provenance.
25. Cognitive-context loss after interruption.

For each test record:

- What was tested.
- Actual source and runtime.
- Setup and triggering conditions.
- Expected behavior.
- Observed behavior.
- Test result.
- Log or artifact reference.
- Remaining uncertainty.

Never report synthetic fixture tests as physical-device verification.

Never report model-call mocks as real inference.

Never report unit-test coverage as end-to-end acceptance.

# PART VIII — OUTPUT AND COMPLETION CONTRACT

## 29. Produce engineering results, not another proposal

The required output is working, integrated, tested project functionality.

Each meaningful increment must include:

**IMPLEMENTED**

Exact source changes, file paths, preserved interfaces, and behavior delivered.

**VERIFIED**

Commands executed, environment, test outcomes, and independent evidence.

**UNVERIFIED**

Claims not yet demonstrated in the actual environment.

**BLOCKED**

The exact missing resource, hardware dependency, authority decision, or incompatible contract.

**REJECTED**

Proposed architecture substitutions or changes that violate the principal's specifications.

**NEXT EXECUTABLE ACTION**

The precise work that resumes the project without another discovery interview.

Do not bury implementation gaps in a polished executive summary.

## 30. Final completion gate

Do not declare Dottie completed until the accepted requirements are demonstrated by:

- Working canonical source.
- Successful compilation/build where applicable.
- Passing current tests.
- Integrated identity, cognition, agent, memory, and execution behavior.
- Durable persistence and successful recovery.
- Enforced memory and authority separation.
- Evidence lineage and certification behavior.
- Independent QA/QI.
- Cognitive-prosthetic acceptance testing.
- Documented remaining platform-specific limitations.

Separate Dottie's completion status from unfinished future GrizOS operating-system ambitions.

Do not redefine success simply because a narrower milestone is easier to finish.

## 31. Mandatory behavior when blocked

If an external dependency is unavailable:

1. Identify the exact dependency and the operation it prevents.
2. Confirm whether another existing authorized path can perform the same work.
3. Preserve the current state.
4. Continue all independent implementation and verification tasks.
5. Leave a precise resume command or action.

Do not ask the principal to perform code-writing, architecture translation, routine source inspection, or testing that the engineering environment can perform.

Do not repeatedly request a file, decision, or fact already available in project history.

## 32. Begin execution immediately

Your first task is **not to write a new architecture**.

Your first task is to recover the active Dottie source tree, verify the Build 7 checkpoint against the current implementation, establish the actual unresolved functional work, and execute the highest-priority authorized repair or integration.

Proceed in this order:

**RECOVER → RECONCILE → IMPLEMENT → INTEGRATE → TEST → INDEPENDENTLY VERIFY → CONTINUE.**

Use the principal's existing specifications as the controlling contract.

No architectural substitutions.

No invented progress.

No unfinished scaffold presented as Dottie.

No handing the implementation back to the principal.

**ENGINEER DOTTIE HILL THROUGH TO THE AUTHORIZED COMPLETION CRITERIA.**

# JOHN WICK: THE QUIET YEARS

<text color="secondary" weight="medium" size="xs">A proposed prequel · Crime drama · Original story concept</text>

<AsyncImageGroup query={["John Wick Keanu Reeves with Helen Wick Bridget Moynahan movie","John Leguizamo as Aurelio John Wick garage scene","John Wick police officer Jimmy Thomas Sadoski movie scene"]} aspectRatio="5:4" layout="carousel"/>

Here's how I would build it.

The opening is the aftermath of the impossible task.

Viggo Tarasov has his empire. The High Table has its arrangements. The criminal underworld is quietly reorganizing around the destruction John just delivered.

And John?

**John wants to know whether the house Helen found has a garage.**

That's the first indication that we're watching a different kind of John Wick movie.

Because the central conflict isn't whether John can kill everybody who comes after him.

It's whether a man who has spent his entire adult life anticipating violence can learn to live somewhere he doesn't have to.

Helen isn't his reward for finishing the impossible task. She is a woman with her own life who has chosen him, and John is determined to become someone who can share that life.

Aurelio becomes the bridge between John's two worlds. He's the guy John still calls when the car makes a funny noise, when he needs something repaired, or when something from the past threatens to follow him home.

And Jimmy?

**Jimmy is how we learn what John looks like to people who aren't criminals.**

## The first meeting

<text color="secondary" size="xs">Original scene · Jimmy's perspective</text>

The first time Officer Jimmy met John Wick, nobody was shooting at anybody.

It was 6:17 on a Tuesday morning.

Jimmy had been dispatched to the little grocery store off the county road. Older man collapsed in the parking lot. Unresponsive. Ambulance en route.

By the time Jimmy arrived, somebody was already doing chest compressions.

Black hair. Dark coat thrown onto the asphalt. Sleeves rolled up.

The man didn't look up.

"How long?" Jimmy asked.

"About four minutes."

"You know CPR?"

"Yes."

"Need me to take over?"

"Yes."

There was something unsettling about how readily the man surrendered his position. No fuss. No argument. He moved aside, kept his eyes on the patient, and let Jimmy take over.

The ambulance arrived less than two minutes later.

The paramedics went to work.

Jimmy stepped back to find the stranger standing beside a black Mustang, staring down at his hands.

"You did good," Jimmy said.

The stranger looked toward the ambulance.

"We'll see."

Jimmy studied him.

"Don't think I've seen you around."

"Just moved here."

"Ah. The place up on the hill?"

"That's right."

"Pretty big house for two people."

The man looked at him.

Jimmy smiled.

"Small town. People talk."

For the first time, the stranger almost smiled.

A woman came out of the store carrying two coffees. She took one look at the ambulance, then at her husband's face.

"John?"

"I'm okay."

She handed him a cup.

"That wasn't my question."

Jimmy watched something remarkable happen.

The man who had been utterly composed during the emergency suddenly looked uncertain about what to say to his wife.

She touched his arm.

"Come on. Let's go home."

Jimmy tipped his head.

"Officer Jimmy."

"John."

"John what?"

"Wick."

"Well, welcome to the neighborhood, Mr. Wick."

"Thank you, Officer."

Jimmy watched them drive away.

He didn't know who John Wick was.

Not yet.

---

**And THAT'S where the story begins.**

Jimmy gradually discovers John's history. Not through a ridiculous secret briefing where the police chief announces the Baba Yaga has moved into town.

Through encounters.

Through professional curiosity.

Through the people who occasionally come looking for John.

Through the terrifying realization that this quiet man with the beautiful wife and the black Mustang has a history that would make half the city's organized crime investigators lose sleep.

And here's the part I'd insist on: **Jimmy learns to trust John because he sees what John chooses not to do.**

We watch a friendship form between two men who live on opposite sides of a very strange boundary.

Meanwhile, Aurelio keeps getting calls.

"John, you bought a house. You got married. You're retired. Why the hell are you calling me at two in the morning?"

"The car's making a noise."

"What kind of noise?"

"A noise."

"Jesus Christ, John."

And beneath all that comedy, Aurelio knows something nobody else knows.

John is genuinely trying.

By the final act, the police chief and the sergeants know who lives up on that hill. They understand the danger attached to his past. They also know what he has done for the people who live there.

There are rules. There is trust. There are boundaries.

And for years, John keeps his promise to Helen.

The film ends on an ordinary evening. John's outside working on the Mustang. Jimmy drives past in his cruiser.

He slows.

"Evening, John."

"Jimmy."

"Everything all right?"

John glances toward the house. Helen's visible through the kitchen window.

"Yeah."

Jimmy nods and drives on.

**For once in his life, John Wick means it.**

And that's why the opening of the first *John Wick* movie hurts so fucking much.

Because now we've actually *lived through the years he lost*.

The impossible task was how John earned his freedom.

**The retirement story is how he learned what freedom was for.**
